newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE WIN ENSURES CLOSE TITLE FIGHT.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE WIN ENSURES CLOSE TITLE FIGHT.

text.p: Jacques Villeneuve's lucky victory in Sunday's Hungarian Grand Prix signalled that he and the Williams team are far from a waning force and will fight tooth and nail to retain their titles this year.

The Canadian was gifted his win and 10 valuable points when former team-mate and defending world champion Damon Hill of Britain suffered a hydraulics failure in his Arrows leading the final lap of the 77-lap race.
He is now only three points behind Michael Schumacher of Ferrari.

"It is going to be a tough fight all the way to the end of the year, very close and very exciting," said Villeneuve's team chief Frank Williams. "Any suggestions that we are out of it are entirely wrong.

"We may not have dominated as we did last year, but sometimes it is a good thing not to win all the time. It has done us some good. It is good for our humility and our determination not to win once in a while.
"But, having said that, I was very sorry for Damon because he drove quite superbly and deserved to win. He was very unfortunate."
Williams said he also felt sorry for his second driver, Heinz-Harald Frentzen of Germany, who might have won but for an unexpected loss of part of his refuelling nozzle when he was leading.

"It was one of those freak things," he said. "The central part of his refuelling coupling, a part of the fuel tank, simply fell out on the lap before he was due to make his pit stop. That is why he had flames briefly at the back of his car."
Frentzen, signed last year to replace Hill, was on a one-stop strategy and running on harder tyres than many of his rivals. The tactic almost paid off handsomely.

But his run of bad luck continued. The German has failed to score a point in three races since finishing second to Schumacher at the French Grand Prix in June -- a sequence which has led many observers to suggest his place in the team is under threat.

Williams said: "He has been unlucky. But I am not worried by his results. Nor is he. We are disappointed, yes, but not worried. And I am not upset by speculation either. We are all right. We are in the championship and it will be a tough fight right to the end."
Williams' faith in Frentzen made it unlikely that he will be replaced next year when he is expected to fulfil the second part of his two-year contract in an unchanged line-up.

Hill, who dominated the race, proved that both he and the previously-struggling Arrows team have the potential to be a competitive combination, particularly on circuits which favour their Bridgestone tyres.
The Japanese tyre manufacturers looked certain to celebrate their first Grand Prix win -- and with it the first for Arrows and Yamaha -- before Hill's misfortune.

Their performance compared well with that of the Mercedes-Benz McLaren team, said to be interested in acquiring Hill's services next season. Both Finn Mika Hakkinen and Briton David Coulthard were forced to retire with unspecified problems.

Hill's future is likely to rest on a choice between the two - staying at Arrows or moving to McLaren - unless Frenchman Alain Prost, his former Williams team-mate, moves quickly to sign him for his team, which will be powered by Peugeot in 1998.

Hakkinen is expected to be the McLaren driver who moves on as he has been with the team for five seasons without a victory. Reports in Finland last weekend suggested he had already signed a contract with another team for next year, but these were denied by his management.
